King Teen Patti architecture

How the game server is put together: what runs where, how one move travels from a tap to every screen, when chips reach the database, and where each rule lives in the code.

Server
Go 1.27, one static binaryevery table is one goroutine
Transport
Socket.IO over websocketour own server, internal/sio
Live state
Redisevery table's snapshot, and nowhere else
Money
PostgreSQLthree checkpoints a hand, append-only ledger
Clients
Flutter (Android, iOS)render snapshots, forward intent

ShapeSystem map

One Go process runs the whole game. It keeps every table in memory, mirrors each table to Redis after every change, and writes chips to PostgreSQL only at three moments of a hand. Players reach it through nginx; the resident bots sit on the same host and connect over loopback.

  • clients
  • transport and edges
  • game rules
  • state and stores
  • outside services
  • operations
The one rule everything followsThe server is the single authority. It shuffles with crypto/rand, deals, checks every bet against a ladder it recomputes itself, decides winners, and sends each player a snapshot with everybody else's cards removed. A client never receives a card or a hidden stack it should not see; it draws snapshots and forwards intent.
PartWhereWhat it does
Game servergo-server/The only server. Rules, rooms, sockets, REST, ledger, metrics. One static binary, bin/gameplay.
Mobile clientflutter-client/The live client. One GameState notifier, one websocket, no rules of its own.
Bot fleetbot-play/Resident bots that keep production's lobby populated. Plain clients of the same protocol.
Toolstools/Practice bots, the ramp load test, and the black-box parity suites.
Browser clientgo-server/public/A vanilla-JS smoke test of the protocol. Hidden in production.
PostgreSQLhost serviceWallets, the chip ledger, accounts, catalogues, table configuration, statistics. Never the table being played.
Redishost serviceThe live store: each table's full snapshot, who sits where, presence, resume offers, statistics waiting to be flushed.
Cloudflare R2private bucketThe catalogue's art. The server only signs ten-minute links; phones download and keep the files.

ShapeInside the server

The module is go-server/, and its packages form layers. The domain, internal/game, holds the rules and knows nothing about HTTP, SQL or Prometheus. It defines small interfaces for what it needs (a ledger, a live store, a clock, a listener for its events) and the packages around it implement them. internal/app is the only place that knows every piece and wires them together.

  • Solid arrows are calls. Dashed arrows mean the domain defines an interface and the package below implements it: game.Ledger by db.Ledger, live.Store by Redis or the in-process store, game.StatsRecorder by stats.Recorder.
  • game must not import metrics, db or socket. Metrics reach it as function hooks; the socket layer reaches it as a game.Listener.
  • Nothing but app and cmd imports socket or app.
  • There is no package-level mutable state. Configuration is read once at boot into one immutable config.Config and passed down.
PackageHolds
cmd/gameplayThe entry point: load .env, config, database, app, listen; SIGTERM handling; the -migrate, -export-table-config, -check-table-config and -version flags.
internal/appComposition: builds every store and service, restores rooms, mounts routes, /health, static files, start and shutdown.
internal/gameTable (the Teen Patti rules engine), RoomManager, the Room interface, Actor/LiveState/Settler, hand ranking, variations, the redacted views, errors and constants.
internal/pokerFour poker variants as rooms beside the Teen Patti tables, built on the same actor shell and the same three checkpoints.
internal/socketThe game protocol: one method per event, the guard, per-viewer emits, the reconnect grace, resume offers.
internal/sioOur own Engine.IO v4 and Socket.IO v5 server on gorilla/websocket. Websocket only.
internal/authREST routes, JWT (HS256), Google, Apple and guest sign-in, rate limits, pagination.
internal/dbThe pgx pool, the embedded migrations, and every transaction: the ledger's checkpoints, users, catalogues, purchases, rewards, friends, reports, statistics.
internal/liveThe live-store interface with two implementations, Redis and in-process memory.
internal/statsThe statistics pipeline: recorder (to Redis), flusher (group commit to PostgreSQL).
internal/config, metrics, utilEnvironment to one Config and the table catalogue contract; every game_* series; uuid, room codes, the JSON logger.

FlowsA table is an actor

Every table owns one goroutine. Anything that reads or changes the table is a closure posted to that goroutine, and the caller waits until it has run. Two moves, a move and a turn timer, a leave and a database answer: none of them can interleave, because they queue. There is no lock inside a table.

The same shell carries Teen Patti tables and poker rooms: Actor (the mailbox), LiveState (the Redis snapshot and its fence) and Settler (the hand-end retry chain) live in actor.go, and both game.Table and poker.Table embed them.

The rules that keep it deadlock-free

  • Exported methods post, unexported ones never do. Table.Act calls t.run(…); t.act, t.bet, t.endHand run on the actor and must not call run again, or the goroutine waits on itself.
  • A listener never calls back into its table. Events (game.Listener) are delivered on the actor goroutine. The kick path, which must remove a player, runs in a goroutine of its own.
  • Timers post. The turn clock, the sideshow clock and the start delay fire through clock.AfterFunc and post a closure. Each carries a token, so a timer that fires after the turn already moved finds a different token and does nothing.
  • Panics stay local. A panic inside one move becomes an internal_error for that move; the table keeps running.
  • Readers that cannot wait use atomics. PlayerCount, IsFull, State and Version are lock-free, so the RoomManager can scan tables while holding its own mutex.
  • The RoomManager's mutex guards only its maps and is never held while a table is called. Each player also has a seat-lock stripe: every door into a seat and every lobby-only wallet change takes it, so a purchase can never land between a join's wallet read and its seat.
After every closureIf the closure changed anything a player can see, the whole table is serialised once and saved to the live store under the next sequence number. A save refused as stale means another process owns the table: it is fenced, accepts nothing more, and is torn down without settling a hand it no longer owns.

FlowsOne move, from the tap to every screen

A bet is the hot path, and it never touches PostgreSQL. The socket layer checks rate limits, the table validates and applies the move in one closure, every viewer gets their own redacted snapshot, and the snapshot is saved to Redis as the closure ends.

  • Refusals carry a code. Every refusal is a GameError{Code, Message} with a snake_case code (not_your_turn, invalid_bet, insufficient_chips …). Clients compare codes, never messages. A refusal arrives twice on purpose, as the ack and as game:error; clients dedupe.
  • Every move is idempotent. The client sends a fresh actionId with each move. The table remembers the ids a player used this hand and refuses a repeat with duplicate_action, so a retried request is never charged twice.
  • Amounts are never trusted. A bet must be exactly a rung of the ladder the table computes (betOptions); anything else is invalid_bet.
  • Seeing your cards is not a move. see is free, allowed off-turn, and does not reset the turn clock.

FlowsJoining a table

The RoomManager owns the lobby: which tables exist, who sits where, and every door into a seat. There are four doors (quick join, join by code, create a private table, and the automatic rejoin after a lapsed connection), and all of them end in the same two steps: reserve the seat in the manager, then AddPlayer on the table's actor.

Check, in orderRefusal codeWhy
Not already seatedalready_in_roomOne seat per player, whichever door they came in by.
Stake is allowedinvalid_stakeThe boot must be one of the lobby's stakes.
Table is on the menutable_not_offeredThe category and boot pair must be a table the lobby opens. Unknown categories fold to seen.
Wallet read under the locksettlement_pending, account_disabledThe seat starts from the wallet as PostgreSQL has it now, read while the player's stripe is held.
Chips cover the bootinsufficient_chipsPoker rooms ask for their buy-in instead.
Stack bandover_entry_cap, below_table_minimumA table can be shut to stacks above a maximum or below a minimum. Exactly the limit is allowed.
  • Which table. Quick join takes the fullest public table of that boot and category that still has a seat (ties: the oldest), so a player arriving finds a game. Only when none has a seat is a new table created.
  • No race for the last seat. The pick and the seat hold happen in one critical section. Fifty players joining at the same instant are routed by the seats that will be taken; nobody is refused table_full by a race.
  • Join by code takes exactly 8 letters or digits, skips the menu checks (any live table can be joined by its code) and skips the stack band for a private table, where the player was invited.
  • Create always opens a private table at the private boot. Its figures come from the private template of that category.
  • Where a new table's rules come from. config.GameConfig.Spec(category, boot, private) is the one answer the table is built from, the lobby card is drawn from, and GET /api/tables serves. The table copies every figure into its own config and snapshot when it opens and never reads the configuration again.

FlowsSwitching tables

A switch moves a seated player sideways to another table of the same boot and category. It is one request to the client and a careful sequence on the server, because the seat must never be lost and chips must never be duplicated on the way.

  • Which table. The other public table of the same kind with the fewest players; ties are drawn with crypto/rand, so where a switcher lands is not predictable. If every other table is full, a new one is opened for the player.
  • Chips travel with the seat, not the wallet. Leaving mid-hand is a checkpoint: the stake already in the pot is banked as lost. The player is re-seated with what the old seat held at that moment. Re-seating from the wallet figure read earlier would hand the stake back.
  • What is and is not checked. The seat must cover the target's boot (or a poker room's buy-in), checked before the seat is given up. The entry cap and the stack band are not applied: those decide who may sit down from the lobby, not who may move sideways.
  • Failure is safe. If the target refuses the seat, the seat at the old table is restored. A table opened for the switch is closed again, so no empty table is left behind.
  • The socket follows. The handler stops listening to the old room before the switch (leaving can destroy it, and "room closed" must not reach a player who is mid-move), then listens to exactly the table the result names.

Leaving, kicks and the sweeper

  • Leave mid-hand is a pack plus checkpoint 2: the stake stays in the pot. If everybody leaves, the last one to leave gets the pot.
  • Idle kick. A turn that times out packs the player and counts a miss; three misses in a row and the table emits kick. The table only emits it; the RoomManager removes the player.
  • Unfunded seats are held for a grace (30 s) between hands so a player can buy chips, then shown out.
  • Consolidation. Every 15 s the sweeper merges lone players waiting on idle public tables of the same kind into the oldest one, and destroys tables that have stood empty for 30 s.
  • Draining. A table restored from Redis keeps the rules frozen in its snapshot. If the configuration has changed since, the table is marked draining: it plays on and can still be joined by code, but matchmaking never sends anyone to it.

FlowsA hand

A table is always in one of four states. Everything else (whose turn it is, a sideshow waiting for its answer, the variation being chosen) is part of the hand inside BETTING.

  • The deal. Each funded seat pays the boot into the pot (in memory), and three cards are dealt from a deck shuffled with crypto/rand. A seat that cannot cover the boot is not dealt in. The first to act is the player on the dealer's left; turns go clockwise by seat index.
  • Blind and seen. Everyone starts blind. A blind bet costs the stake, a seen bet twice the stake. After four blind bets a player's cards turn over for them automatically.
  • The ladder. The server computes the legal amounts for the player on turn (betOptions): the chaal, then doublings up to the table's limits and the player's stack. The client shows exactly that list; any other amount is refused.
  • The turn clock. 25 seconds. A turn that runs out packs the player and counts a missed turn; three in a row removes them from the table.
  • How a hand ends. Everyone but one has packed; or two players are left and one pays for a show; or the table's round cap or pot cap forces a showdown; or a player fires a missile (three or more players still in), which shows every hand at once.
  • Sideshow. A seen player may ask the player who acted just before them to compare hands privately. The loser packs. Nothing is charged, and the asked player has 6 seconds to accept or decline. A Force Sideshow costs a hammer and cannot be declined.

Who wins an exact tie

Hands are ranked by one function, Evaluate: high card, pair, color, sequence, pure sequence, trail. Suits never break a tie, so two hands can be exactly equal. The pot is never split; the rule depends on how the comparison was started.

ComparisonAn exact tie goes
Showagainst the player who called the show
Sideshow, Force Sideshowagainst the player who asked
Missileto the player who fired it, when their hand ties for the best
Round cap, pot cap, or a tie among the other playersto the tied seat nearest the dealer going clockwise, the dealer's own seat first

What each player is sent

After every change the table emits state, and the socket layer sends each viewer their own copy, built by serializeFor(viewer) in view.go. There is no room-wide snapshot.

  • you.cards only once the viewer has seen their cards; every other seat carries only cardCount.
  • On blind and variation tables, and in poker rooms, other players' chips are null, never 0.
  • you.options (the ladder and which keys are live) exists only for the player on turn.
  • Cards are revealed to everyone only at a showdown, and a sideshow's cards go to its two players alone.

Variation tables and poker rooms

A variation table deals as usual, then the first player to act has 10 seconds to choose the hand's variation (Muflis, AK47, Joker, Hukam, Lowest Joker, Highest Joker, or 5-Card); if the clock runs out the server chooses Muflis. There is still one ranking: each variation is a wild-card rule and a comparison direction laid over Evaluate (variation.go).

The poker family (3-Card Poker, 5-Card Draw, Texas Hold'em, Omaha) lives in internal/poker. A poker room implements the same game.Room interface, runs on the same actor shell, and banks money at the same three checkpoints; it has its own events (poker:*) and its own five-card evaluator.

FlowsMoney: three checkpoints

PostgreSQL holds the wallet (users.chips) and an append-only audit of every movement (chip_ledger). A bet is not a database transaction, and neither is the deal. The wallet is brought up to date at exactly three moments, each taking that player's chips as the live table has them.

MomentLedger reasonaction_idWho is written
A player packshand_packed<handId>:packed:<userId>that player
A player leaves, switches or is kickedhand_left<handId>:left:<userId>that player
The hand endshand_win / hand_loss<handId>:settle:<userId>everyone still at the table
The winner's taxtable_tax<handId>:tax:<userId>the winner, in the same transaction

Why it is safe

  • Deltas, never absolutes. Each checkpoint writes seat chips now − chips as last written. A reward or purchase that credited the wallet meanwhile is therefore never overwritten.
  • action_id is UNIQUE, and that is a mechanism. If a settle commits but its answer is lost, the table resends the same request. The replay hits the unique index, the whole transaction rolls back, and the table reads duplicate_action as the success it is. The winner is never paid twice.
  • Resolve once, record twice. A player who packed gets a hand_packed row when the money moves and a zero-delta hand_loss row at the hand end, which records the outcome.
  • The ledger is append-only. A trigger refuses every UPDATE and DELETE on chip_ledger. The one exception is the purge job, which removes hand rows older than ten minutes inside its own guarded transaction.
  • Chips cannot change while seated except at a checkpoint. Every lobby-only wallet change (a chip-priced picture, the Lucky Draw, a reward claim, account deletion) runs under the player's seat stripe and is refused seated at a table. A chip pack bought at a table credits the database and tops up the seat together.
  • The winning tax. At a public Teen Patti table the winner pays their rate on winnings (the pot less their own chips) of 50 Lakh or more. The seat is credited the pot less the tax; the ledger writes the win gross and the tax as its own row, so a hand's rows still sum to zero.
The invariant to keep trueSUM(chip_ledger.delta) per user equals users.chips. Losing Redis loses the hands in play and nothing else: every player keeps what PostgreSQL last knew. Chips can be un-made by an interrupted hand, never created.

FlowsStatistics: Redis first, then one group commit

A player's record (hands played, won and lost, winnings, the winning tax they paid, the hands they held, the variations they played) is not written by the money transactions. Tables record each committed hand's counters in Redis, and a flusher adds them to PostgreSQL in batches, one transaction per batch.

  1. At the hand's end the table works out a HandStats per player while the cards and rules are still there, and carries them on the settle request.
  2. Only when the ledger's transaction has committed does the table hand them to its StatsRecorder. A replay (duplicate_action) records nothing, so a hand counts at most once.
  3. The recorder queues them off the actor and writes them to Redis: one hash per player, kt:stats:<userId>, one field per counter such as TEEN_PATTI:hands_won or VARIATION:total_tax_paid.
  4. Every STATS_FLUSH_MS (10 s) the flusher moves up to 500 players' counters out atomically under a new batch id.
  5. It adds them in one PostgreSQL transaction: the batch's receipt in stats_flushes first, then one upsert into player_stats and one into player_variation_stats.
  6. Only after the commit is the batch finished in Redis. A crash in between replays the batch, and its receipt makes the replay add nothing.
  7. Every account read sums the player's rows, so the figures trail play by at most one flush interval.

The winning tax a player has paid is their own figure: it is on their account (totalTaxPaid) and in their own Stats drawer, and no other player's profile carries any chip figure.

FlowsDropped connections

Phones lose their network, get locked, and switch apps. A seat survives all of that for a while, and after that the way back to the table survives a while longer.

  • The handshake carries the JWT (handshake.auth.token) and the app's platform and version. It is refused with a code (invalid_session, account_disabled, session_replaced, update_required, maintenance) and such a refusal is final; a network failure is retried by the client.
  • One live socket per account, one signed-in device. Every login counts a new session (user_sessions.version, signed into the token as sv). A newer login ends the older device's socket with session:replaced, and the new device's connection takes over the seat.
  • The grace. When a socket drops, the seat is marked disconnected and held for 60 seconds. The turn clocks keep running. Reconnect inside the grace and the server sends room:joined with the live hand.
  • The resume offer. When the grace runs out the player leaves the table, and the table is offered back for 10 minutes: the next session:ready carries resume, and the app rejoins with room:joinCode. An idle kick of a player with no live socket leaves the same offer.
  • The app helps. Sent to the background while seated, the Flutter app closes its socket after 8 seconds, which starts the server's grace at once instead of letting three turn clocks run out unanswered.
  • Silent drops are noticed by the Engine.IO heartbeat (ping every 20 s, 25 s timeout).

FlowsBoot, restore and shutdown

Configuration is read once. A value that does not parse stops the binary with the key named, and production refuses to start on a weak JWT secret or without the R2 keys. Everything that is built afterwards holds the same immutable Config for the life of the process.

  • Migrations run at every boot. There is no schema history table: the server applies every embedded script every time, so each one is idempotent. gameplay -migrate runs the same step alone, which is what a deploy does before it restarts anything.
  • The table catalogue (engines, categories and every lobby table with its figures) is read once, from PostgreSQL when TABLE_CONFIG_SOURCE=db, otherwise composed from the environment. An edit to the rows applies at the next restart, to tables opened after it.
  • Restore. Every table snapshot in Redis is rebuilt as a running actor. The first bytes of a snapshot say which game it is, and the matching factory restores it. Seats come back disconnected and are held for the grace; timers resume with what was left of their deadlines. A turn whose deadline passed while the process was down gets a fresh clock rather than an instant timeout.
  • Without Redis (REDIS_URL empty) the live store is in-process memory: a single instance whose tables do not survive a restart. Players rejoin; nothing is reconstructed.
  • Shutdown. On SIGTERM the socket server closes first. With Redis, every table is suspended: its clocks stop, a final snapshot is saved, and the next process resumes the hand where it stopped. With the in-process store, every live pot is settled instead (to the first active seat, reason all_left), because nothing would come back. Then the statistics still waiting are flushed and the process exits, all within max(8 s, statement timeout + 5 s).
Two owners, neverEvery snapshot is saved under a sequence number with a compare-and-set. A process that finds a newer sequence than its own knows another process owns that table, and stops touching it.

ReferenceData model

Two stores with a strict division. PostgreSQL holds what must never be lost: money, accounts, audit and configuration. Redis holds the game being played. No table in PostgreSQL is game state.

PostgreSQL: 44 tables

GroupTablesNotes
Accountsusers, user_sessions, user_milestonesThe wallet is users.chips, with diamonds, hammers and missiles beside it. Rows are never deleted; deleting an account empties and pseudonymises it.
Moneychip_ledger, diamond_purchases, hammer_purchases, hammer_spends, missile_purchases, missile_spends, badge_purchaseschip_ledger.action_id is UNIQUE and the table is append-only. The purchase tables are replay guards keyed on the store's token.
Cataloguesprofile_pictures, user_profile_pictures, table_pictures, user_table_pictures, user_table_choice, emojis, user_emojisWhat can be bought with chips, hammers or diamonds, and who owns what. Art lives in R2; rows hold its location.
Table configurationtable_engines, table_categories, table_settings, table_configsEngines, categories and every lobby table with every figure it plays by. Read once at boot.
Statisticsplayer_stats, player_variation_stats, stats_flushesOne row per player per game bucket; written only by the flusher's group commit.
Progressionplayer_levels, badges, user_badges, xp_sources, xp_settings, player_xp, player_xp_claims, player_xp_missions50 levels by XP and badges held beside them. The winning-tax rate is the lowest of the level's and the badges'.
Rewardslucky_draws, lucky_draw_slots, user_lucky_draws, welcome_rewards, reward_programs, reward_program_rewards, user_reward_claims, user_reward_progressConfiguration rows plus an idempotent history of what each player was granted.
Socialfriend_requests, friendships, player_reportsThe friends graph and moderation reports. Presence is never stored here.
Operationsapp_versionsMinimum and latest app version and maintenance per platform, read while the server runs.
  • Migrations. internal/db/migration/ holds V1.0.0__baseline.sql (all structure) and V1.0.1__seed.sql (rows), then row-only seed files. All of them run at every boot, so everything is idempotent. A new column is written twice: in its CREATE TABLE, and in a catalogue-guarded block that adds it to a database built before it.
  • Timestamps are epoch milliseconds in BIGINT columns; money is int64 end to end.

Redis: the live store

Key (prefix kt:)Holds
table:<roomId>, tablesThe full server-side snapshot of one table (cards, bets, deadlines) with its sequence number; the index of tables.
chat:<roomId>The room's recent chat lines.
seat:<userId>Which room a player is seated in.
playing:<userId>, onlinePresence for the friends list: the game and variant being played (never a room id), and who is connected.
resume:<userId>The table offered back after a lapsed connection.
summary:<roomId>, lobby:<category:boot>Published table summaries for matchmaking.
stats:<userId>, stats:dirty, stats:batch:<id>Statistics waiting for the next flush, and batches taken but not yet committed.
xpplay:<userId>Active play time inside the player's daily XP window.

ReferenceWire protocol

Realtime traffic is Socket.IO over a websocket at /socket.io/; everything else is REST under /api with a JWT in the Authorization header. Every socket request is acknowledged with {ok: true, …} or {ok: false, code, message}. The full contract is in go-server/PORT_NOTES/specs/spec-socket-protocol.md.

Client to server

EventPayloadDoes
room:quickJoin{bootAmount?, category?}Sit at the fullest open table of that kind, or open one.
room:create{isPrivate, category?}Open a private table.
room:joinCode{code}Join a table by its 8-character code.
room:switch{}Move to another table of the same kind.
room:leave{}Leave the table.
game:action{action, amount?, actionId?}see, chaal, raise, pack, show, sideshow, forceSideshow, missile.
game:sideshowRespond{accept}Answer a sideshow request.
game:selectVariation{variation}Choose the hand's variation.
game:selectCards{cards: [3]}Choose three of five under 5-Card.
poker:action{action, amount?, cards?, actionId?}A move in a poker room.
chat:message, chat:emoji{text}, {emojiId}Table chat, with its own rate limit.

Errors are always {error: code, message}. Signed-in routes pass, in order: the app version gate (426 update_required, 503 maintenance), the token, the disabled-account check and the single-session check. Lists that grow with a player are paged, 20 at a time.

Every setting is an environment key with a default, listed in go-server/.env.example and parsed once by internal/config. Table rules can come from PostgreSQL instead.

ReferenceDeploy and observe

  • Releases are tags. go-server/vX.Y.Z for the server, flutter-client/vX.Y.Z for the app, bot-play/vX.Y.Z for the bots. ops/build.sh stamps the tag into the binary, and GET /health reports it, so checking what production runs is one curl.
  • One command deploys. ops/deploy.sh <tag> on the host: fetch, check the tag out, build, run the new binary's -migrate before any restart, restart, wait for /health to report the tag, and roll back by itself if it does not.
  • Metrics. GET /metrics exposes every game_* series (sockets, tables, moves, timings, the ledger, the live store, the stats flusher) and the Go runtime. No user id, room id, table code, name or IP is ever a label value.
  • Dashboards and logs. Prometheus, Grafana, Loki and Alloy run on the game host (ops/monitoring/). The server logs JSON lines; a refused login, a refused table write and a table marked draining each have their own line.
  • Tests. go test -race ./... (table rules on a fake clock, database suites on throwaway schemas, real sockets through a test client), the black-box parity suites in tools/parity, and flutter analyze with flutter test.

ReferenceWhere to change things

A rule of Teen Patti
internal/game/table.go; view.go if clients must see it; a test in internal/game on the fake clock.
Hand ranking or a variation
handrank.go, variation.go. One Evaluate; never a second ranking.
Matchmaking, switch, sweeping
internal/game/roommanager.go.
A lobby table or its figures
A row in table_configs (db mode), then a restart. Check with GET /api/tables.
A socket event
internal/socket/wire.go (the payload structs) and handler.go (register it behind guard).
A REST route
internal/auth/http.go (routes) and handlers.go.
Anything that moves chips
internal/db, with a chip_ledger row under a unique action_id; if it is lobby-only, run it inside RoomManager.WhileUnseated.
A table or column
internal/db/migration/V1.0.0__baseline.sql, idempotent; a column twice (CREATE TABLE and a guarded block).
A player statistic
game/stats.go (what a hand counts), stats/codec.go (the Redis field), db/stats.go (the flush and the read).
A metric
internal/metrics/names.go; feed it from the socket layer or a hook, never from game.
A poker rule
internal/poker (hand.go, variant.go, eval5.go).
What the app draws
flutter-client/lib: state/game_state.dart, net/game_connection.dart, screens/, widgets/.

King Teen Patti backend architecture. The exhaustive reference is CLAUDE.md at the repository root; the long form of this page is docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.
